scenes.tts: In chapter 1, we cut the links in a drawing, and the doublets slid apart instead of bending. Now turn the question around. When a real cilium stops, which part broke, and where in the body does it show?
scenes.visual: Open on chapter 1's right-hand machine, already moving: two doublets, each a blue A-tubule fused to a purple B-tubule, with yellow dynein arms stepping and red cut marks over the orange links, sliding apart. As the narrator turns the question, the pair shrinks into a small inset at top left and a simple grey human body outline fades in, filling the frame height, with three empty white circles at the airway, the groin and an arm's blood vessel. A large white question mark pulses over the body. Small label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: In chapter 1, we cut the links in a drawing, and the doublets slid apart instead of bending. Now turn the question around. When a real cilium stops, which part broke, and where in the body does it show?

scenes.tts: Summers and Gibbons tested that idea in 1971. They took axonemes from sea urchin sperm. They briefly treated them with trypsin, a protein-cutting enzyme, then added zero point one millimolar ATP.
scenes.caption: Summers and Gibbons tested that idea in 1971. They took axonemes from sea urchin sperm. They briefly treated them with trypsin, a protein-cutting enzyme, then added 0.1 mM ATP.
scenes.visual: The body outline slides aside; a round dish fills the frame, labelled '1971: Summers and Gibbons'. A cartoon sea urchin drops a few sperm whose tails peel off as grey rods labelled 'axonemes'. Small red blocks labelled 'trypsin' briefly touch the rods as the protein connectors resisting sliding fade and break, marked 'schematic'; do not imply selective cleavage of one identified complex. Then yellow sparks labelled 'ATP 0.1 mM' fall into the dish. Keep the rods drifting gently.
scenes.narration: Summers and Gibbons tested that idea in 1971. They took axonemes from sea urchin sperm. They briefly treated them with trypsin, a protein-cutting enzyme, then added 0.1 mM ATP.

scenes.tts: Under dark-field microscopy, the axonemes did not beat. Groups of doublets slid out of the bundle. That dish test became a standard way to ask whether a flagellum's motors work.
scenes.visual: The dish view switches to a dark-field look: black background, rods glowing white. One rod splays as groups of glowing doublets telescope lengthwise out of the bundle, while none of them curve. A small label 'did not beat' sits beside it. Then a teal tag 'test: do the motors work?' attaches to the dish, which shrinks to a small icon at the left edge, kept for the rest of the film.
scenes.narration: Under dark-field microscopy, the axonemes did not beat. Groups of doublets slid out of the bundle. That dish test became a standard way to ask whether a flagellum's motors work.

scenes.tts: Now the body. In 1976, Björn Afzelius described four men whose sperm did not swim. Electron microscopy indicated that the dynein arms, small projections on each outer doublet, were missing from their cilia.
scenes.visual: Return to the grey body outline. Four simple sperm cartoons appear at the groin circle, tails straight and still, labelled '1976: sperm do not swim'. Zoom on one tail into the familiar 9+2 cross-section ring: blue A-tubules, purple B-tubules, central pair. The yellow dynein arms that sat on each A-tubule fade to dashed outlines labelled 'dynein arms missing'. Keep the diagram drifting slightly without rotating it.
scenes.narration: Now the body. In 1976, Björn Afzelius described four men whose sperm did not swim. Electron microscopy indicated that the dynein arms, small projections on each outer doublet, were missing from their cilia.

scenes.tts: Sperm tails and the cilia lining the airways are built on the same basic axoneme. So predict: if the dynein arms are missing, what else should fail?
scenes.visual: Draw a second 9+2 ring beside the first, labelled 'airway cilium', with the same blue, purple and dashed-yellow colouring; an orange bracket joins the two rings, labelled 'same basic axoneme'. Light the airway circle on the body outline with a pulsing white question mark. Show the question in large white text across the top: 'Arms missing: what else fails?'
scenes.narration: Sperm tails and the cilia lining the airways are built on the same basic axoneme. So predict: if the dynein arms are missing, what else should fail?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card, both rings and the lit airway circle. Only the dashed yellow outlines shimmer faintly and the rings pulse gently without rotating; reveal nothing.

scenes.tts: Three of the four men also had frequent bronchitis and sinusitis. Their airway cilia were not moving mucus, a sweep called mucociliary transport. One missing part disrupted motion in two organs.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the airway circle: a row of cilia standing on a cell sheet under a pale mucus layer, with a few dark dust specks in it. In a normal inset, cilia beat in a wave and green arrows carry the mucus upward. In the patients' view the cilia stand still, the green arrows fade and the specks stay put. Label 'mucociliary transport'. Then both lit circles, airway and sperm, link back by orange lines to one dashed dynein-arm icon.
scenes.narration: Three of the four men also had frequent bronchitis and sinusitis. Their airway cilia were not moving mucus, a sweep called mucociliary transport. One missing part disrupted motion in two organs.

scenes.tts: The match is not perfect: sperm and airway cilia differ in some dynein parts. And one mutation need not act the same everywhere. In mice lacking a protein called Cfap53, cilia on the embryonic node stopped completely. Windpipe and brain-ventricle cilia still beat, but abnormally.
scenes.caption: The match is not perfect: sperm and airway cilia differ in some dynein parts. And one mutation need not act the same everywhere. In mice lacking a protein called Cfap53, cilia on the embryonic node stopped completely. Windpipe and brain-ventricle cilia still beat, but abnormally.
scenes.visual: Replace the body outline with a cartoon mouse outline. One missing-part block labelled 'Cfap53 missing' sends three arrows to three small panels in a row: 'node' (a small pit on the embryo, cilia frozen, a red stop mark), 'windpipe' and 'brain ventricles' (cilia still waving but with an uneven, stuttering beat). Label the row 'one mutation, different effects'. Mark the panels 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The match is not perfect: sperm and airway cilia differ in some dynein parts. And one mutation need not act the same everywhere. In mice lacking a protein called Cfap53, cilia on the embryonic node stopped completely. Windpipe and brain-ventricle cilia still beat, but abnormally.

scenes.tts: The instrument matters too. Patients with D N A H eleven mutations had normal-looking nasal cilia by conventional electron microscopy. Three-dimensional electron tomography found less outer-arm volume near the base.
scenes.caption: The instrument matters too. Patients with DNAH11 mutations had normal-looking nasal cilia by conventional electron microscopy. Three-dimensional electron tomography found less outer-arm volume near the base.
scenes.visual: Two side-by-side viewing boxes of the same nasal cilium. Left box, labelled 'conventional EM', shows a flat 9+2 ring with all yellow arms drawn, and a green tick 'looks normal'. Right box, labelled 'electron tomography', shows the cilium as a 3D tube that rotates; near its base the outer yellow arms shrink to smaller blocks labelled 'less outer-arm volume'. A small tag reads 'one study'.
scenes.narration: The instrument matters too. Patients with DNAH11 mutations had normal-looking nasal cilia by conventional electron microscopy. Three-dimensional electron tomography found less outer-arm volume near the base.

scenes.tts: Crawling cells break the same way. Chapter 1's clutch needed integrins to grip. Neutrophils without a working integrin of the beta two family grip the vessel wall poorly. They largely fail to leave the blood, so infections are poorly controlled.
scenes.caption: Crawling cells break the same way. Chapter 1's clutch needed integrins to grip. Neutrophils without a working integrin of the β2 family grip the vessel wall poorly. They largely fail to leave the blood, so infections are poorly controlled.
scenes.visual: Pan to the arm circle on the human outline and zoom into a blood vessel: a red-tinted tube with a pink wall, and white neutrophil cartoons rolling along inside. Bring back chapter 1's orange integrin clutch blocks on a normal neutrophil, which grips the wall, flattens and squeezes out toward a cluster of green bacteria dots. Then show a neutrophil with dashed integrin blocks labelled 'beta-2 integrin defective': it fails to arrest firmly and is carried away, while the bacteria dots multiply. Label 'leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I'.
scenes.narration: Crawling cells break the same way. Chapter 1's clutch needed integrins to grip. Neutrophils without a working integrin of the β2 family grip the vessel wall poorly. They largely fail to leave the blood, so infections are poorly controlled.

scenes.tts: Read a phenotype backward, tissue by tissue. Ask which machine failed, which part is defective, which tissue you examined, and with what instrument. Motors and constraints from chapter 1 become the places to look.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full human outline with all three lit circles: airway, sperm, blood vessel. From each, an orange arrow runs backward to its defective part: the dashed dynein-arm icon, and the dashed integrin clutch block. Behind them, restore chapter 1's split bench faintly: the teal actin edge on the left and the bending axoneme on the right, with the orange constraint gate and the magenta motor-control dial. Everything keeps drifting slowly.
scenes.narration: Read a phenotype backward, tissue by tissue. Ask which machine failed, which part is defective, which tissue you examined, and with what instrument. Motors and constraints from chapter 1 become the places to look.

scenes.visual: End card over the dim body outline and carried bench: 'Read a phenotype backward, tissue by tissue.' Large and centred, with the axoneme gently flexing and speckles drifting behind it.
